## Website Designer in Pune: How the CSS :has() Selector Is Replacing JavaScript in 2026

A website designer in Pune building interactive interfaces in 2026 finally has a browser feature that removes one of the most common reasons to reach for JavaScript at all: styling an element based on what's inside it, or near it. The `:has()` selector — sometimes called the "parent selector" web developers asked for since CSS existed — reached Baseline Widely Available status in June 2026, meaning it now works reliably across every browser your visitors are actually using, without a fallback or a polyfill. If your design or development team hasn't already folded it into how components get built, this is the point where it stops being an experimental trick and starts being the default way to solve a specific, very common class of problem.

### What :has() actually does

Ordinary CSS selectors describe an element by what it is, or by what comes before it in the document — a paragraph, a link, an element after a heading. What CSS has never been able to do on its own is style an element based on what it *contains*, or what comes *after* it. `:has()` closes that gap. Written as `selector:has(other-selector)`, it matches the first selector only when it contains (or is followed by, depending on how it's combined) something matching the second.

A form section can now be highlighted red the moment one of its inputs is marked invalid — `.form-group:has(input:invalid)` — with a single line of CSS, no JavaScript event listener, no `classList.add()` call on blur. A card component can change its own layout when it contains an image versus when it doesn't. A heading immediately followed by a paragraph can be styled differently from one followed by a list, using `h2:has(+ p)` — a "preceding sibling" style relationship that was flatly impossible to express in CSS before this.

### Where it actually saves work

The realistic value of `:has()` for a design and development team isn't that it makes something newly possible that JavaScript couldn't already do — it's that it deletes a specific, repetitive category of JavaScript that exists purely to toggle a class on a parent element in response to a change in a child element. That pattern shows up constantly in real interfaces:

- **Form validation styling.** Highlighting an entire field group — label, input, helper text — when the input inside it fails validation, without wiring up a JS listener on every field.
- **Empty-state styling.** Showing a "no results" message layout when a results container has no matching children, using `:has()` combined with `:not()` — for example, styling a product grid differently when it contains zero product cards.
- **Conditional layout based on content.** A card that reserves space for an image differently depending on whether an image is actually present in the markup, rather than always reserving the space and hiding a broken image icon.
- **Sidebar and navigation state.** Highlighting a parent menu item when any of its child links matches the current page, replacing what used to be a small JavaScript routine run on every route change.
- **Dark-mode and theme toggles scoped to content.** Styling a container differently when it has a child with a specific data attribute, useful for CMS-driven pages where content editors add blocks that need different treatment without a developer touching the stylesheet each time.

In each of these cases, the JavaScript being replaced wasn't complex, but it was one more event listener, one more place a bug could creep in, and one more thing that broke silently if a class name changed elsewhere in the codebase. Moving that logic into CSS means it lives with the rest of the component's styling, is visible in one place, and can't drift out of sync with a JavaScript file maintained separately.

### Browser support, in practical terms

As of mid-2026, global browser support for `:has()` exceeds 93% of traffic. Safari shipped it first, in Safari 15.4 back in March 2022; Chrome and Edge followed in version 105 the same year; Firefox was the last major holdout, adding support in version 121 in December 2023. Practically, every browser released in the last two to three years supports it, which is why it crossed the Baseline threshold this year — Baseline status specifically means a feature works consistently enough across the major engines that a team can rely on it without checking caniuse.com before every project.

The remaining roughly 7% is mostly older Android WebView instances and a long tail of outdated browser versions still in use on older devices — a real number, but not one that, on its own, justifies avoiding a feature that saves this much repetitive JavaScript. For the sites and apps where that last sliver of unsupported traffic genuinely matters — a banking portal or a government-facing service with an unusually old device base, for instance — the fix isn't to avoid `:has()` altogether. It's to write base styles that work without it, then layer the enhancement on top using a feature query: `@supports selector(:has(img)) { /* enhanced styles here */ }`. Everyone gets a functional page; supported browsers get the nicer, JavaScript-free version.

### A performance caveat worth knowing before you use it everywhere

`:has()` isn't free, and it's worth a website designer in Pune understanding why before scattering it across every component without thought. Browser engines have to re-evaluate a `:has()` condition whenever the DOM changes in a way that could affect it — because unlike most selectors, which only look at an element's own state, `:has()` depends on the state of its descendants or siblings, which can change independently of the element itself. Anchoring a `:has()` selector to something very broad — `body:has(.some-class)`, for example — means any DOM mutation anywhere inside `<body>` triggers a re-check, which on a large, frequently-updating page can measurably affect rendering performance.

The practical guidance is straightforward: scope `:has()` selectors as narrowly as you can. Prefer `.form-group:has(input:invalid)` over a rule anchored higher up the tree that happens to produce the same visual result. For most marketing sites, brochure pages and even moderately complex e-commerce catalogues, this is a non-issue at the scale involved. It starts to matter on data-heavy dashboards or pages with hundreds of frequently-updating DOM nodes, which is a smaller slice of what most Pune businesses are actually building.

### A concrete before-and-after

It's easier to see the value with an actual comparison. Take a common e-commerce pattern: highlighting a product card's border when its "Add to Cart" button is hovered or focused, so the whole card feels responsive rather than just the button. Before `:has()`, this required either wrapping the button and card in extra markup that let a CSS sibling selector reach the button's state, or a small JavaScript snippet adding and removing a class on `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` and `focus`/`blur`:

```
// The JavaScript version
button.addEventListener('mouseenter', () => card.classList.add('is-active'));
button.addEventListener('mouseleave', () => card.classList.remove('is-active'));
button.addEventListener('focus', () => card.classList.add('is-active'));
button.addEventListener('blur', () => card.classList.remove('is-active'));
```

With `:has()`, the entire thing collapses into one CSS rule, with no event listeners, no risk of a listener leaking on component unmount in a single-page app, and no dependency on JavaScript having loaded and executed before the interaction works:

```
.product-card:has(button:hover, button:focus) {
  border-color: var(--accent);
}
```

The CSS version also has a property the JavaScript version doesn't: it works correctly the instant the page's stylesheet loads, before any JavaScript bundle has parsed or executed. On a slower mobile connection — still the reality for a large share of Indian shoppers browsing on 4G — that gap between "page is visually painted" and "JavaScript has taken over interactivity" is exactly where a lot of janky, half-working interfaces come from. Removing interactions from that gap entirely is a small but real reliability improvement, not just a tidier codebase, and it's the same category of fix that shows up in a [technical SEO and page-speed audit](/services/seo) when a slow Interaction to Next Paint score traces back to too much client-side JavaScript running just to keep the interface in sync with itself.

### Handling empty states without a template conditional

A second pattern worth calling out specifically for Indian business sites: empty states on search results, filtered product grids, and dashboard widgets. Traditionally, showing a "No results found" message when a container has no matching children requires either a server-side conditional in your templating layer or a JavaScript check that counts child nodes after a filter runs. Combining `:has()` with `:not()` lets CSS handle this directly:

```
.results-grid:not(:has(.product-card)) .empty-state {
  display: block;
}
```

This rule shows the empty-state message only when the results grid contains zero product cards — no counting logic, no extra JavaScript branch, and no risk of the message flashing briefly before a script finishes checking. For a WooCommerce or Shopify storefront customised with a Pune-based agency's own templates, this is a small change that removes a whole category of "empty state showed for a second even though there were results" bugs that testers routinely catch late in a project.

### The accessibility and SEO angle nobody markets, but matters

There's a secondary benefit to moving interaction logic out of JavaScript and into CSS that rarely makes it into feature announcements: less client-side JavaScript generally means less that can go wrong for a user on an older device, a slow connection, or assistive technology that doesn't execute scripts the way a modern desktop browser does. A validation state driven by `:has(input:invalid)` is visible to a screen reader through the same accessible-name and state mechanisms as the input itself, without a developer having to remember to also update an `aria-live` region via JavaScript when the class toggles. It's not a replacement for deliberate accessibility work, but it removes one more place where accessibility support quietly breaks because a script didn't run, was blocked by an extension, or threw an unrelated error earlier on the page that halted execution.

### What this means for choosing a website designer or developer

If you're briefing a redesign or a new build in 2026, this is a reasonable, concrete question to ask a prospective website designer in Pune: how much custom JavaScript does their typical component library rely on for things that modern CSS can now do natively? A team still writing a dedicated `onChange` handler purely to toggle a validation class, or a script that walks the DOM to highlight the active navigation item, is carrying maintenance weight that a `:has()`-based approach removes — fewer lines of JavaScript to test, fewer places where a class name typo silently breaks a feature, and often a small but real page-weight and performance improvement from shipping less script.

This isn't a reason to distrust a team that hasn't already rewritten every component to use `:has()` — plenty of stable, well-built sites will migrate gradually rather than all at once, and that's a sensible approach. It is a reasonable signal, though, if a team is unfamiliar with the feature entirely or dismisses it as "still experimental," since that status changed with June 2026's Baseline milestone. The same question is worth asking about the other native browser features that have crossed similar milestones recently — container queries, the Popover API, CSS anchor positioning — since a team keeping current with browser capability tends to ship smaller, more maintainable stylesheets across the board, not just in the one feature you happened to ask about.

### Rolling it into an existing build process

For teams using Sass, PostCSS, or a component framework like React or Vue with CSS Modules, `:has()` needs no special tooling — it's plain CSS and passes through a preprocessor or bundler exactly like any other selector. The one thing worth checking is your linter configuration: older `stylelint` presets sometimes flag `:has()` as an unknown or experimental selector by default, which is a leftover from before its Baseline status and is safe to update once you confirm your project's supported-browser list. If your build pipeline runs automated CSS audits as part of CI, it's worth a five-minute check that this isn't silently failing a build over a selector that's now perfectly safe to ship.

### Frequently asked questions

**Does :has() replace all the JavaScript in a typical interactive component?**
No — it replaces a specific, narrow category: class-toggling on a parent in response to a change in a child or sibling. Genuine interactivity that depends on user events, animations with timed sequencing, or anything requiring state that persists across page loads still needs JavaScript. The realistic win is smaller and more maintainable components, not a JavaScript-free website.

**Is it safe to use on a WordPress site built with a page builder?**
Generally yes, since `:has()` is a browser feature rather than something tied to a specific CMS or builder — it works the same whether your CSS is hand-written or generated by Elementor, Divi or a similar tool. The practical limitation is usually the page builder's own custom-CSS interface, which may or may not make it easy to write a selector this specific; a developer with direct theme or child-theme access has more room to use it well.

**What should I ask my developer to check before relying on it for something important?**
Ask which specific interactions they're using it for, and whether there's a fallback for the roughly 7% of browsers still outside Baseline support — particularly if a meaningful share of your audience is on older Android devices, which is common for budget-conscious consumer audiences in tier-2 and tier-3 Indian cities. For anything load-bearing (form validation, checkout state), a tested `@supports` fallback is worth the small extra effort.

**Does adopting :has() require a full site rebuild?**
No. It's additive — existing CSS keeps working exactly as before, and `:has()` rules can be introduced incrementally, component by component, during normal maintenance or a partial redesign rather than requiring a wholesale rebuild.

**Can I mock this behaviour in Figma before a developer builds it?**
Not directly — design tools model visual states as separate artboards or component variants rather than conditional relationships between elements, so there's no native Figma equivalent to "style this card when it contains a specific child." The practical workflow is to describe the *condition* in your design handoff notes (for example, "card border highlights when the button is hovered or focused") rather than trying to represent every resulting state as a separate frame, and let the developer implement the actual relationship in CSS. This is a case where the design system's written interaction spec matters more than the static mockup.

### Where to take this next

If your current site relies on a lot of small JavaScript utilities just to keep parent elements in sync with their children — validation states, active-menu highlighting, conditional card layouts — a short technical review can usually identify which of those can be safely replaced with `:has()` today, and which genuinely need to stay as JavaScript.
